messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Mai was nineteen and working as a hairdresser at a salon in a strip mall when the accident happened. She had been driving home after a long shift, her mind still half on the client who had wanted a complicated balayage, when she saw the boy—maybe seven years old—break away from his mother on the sidewalk and sprint straight into the crosswalk without looking. Mai slammed the brakes, but the car hit him. The sound of the impact was a dull, heavy thud that seemed to come from inside her own chest, and then the screaming started—the mother's scream, the boy's thin wail, the screech of the tires on the asphalt still ringing in her ears. She got out of the car and saw him lying on the ground, his leg bent at an angle that made her stomach turn. She dialed 911 with shaking hands, and while she waited, she kept saying "I'm sorry" over and over, but the words felt useless. The boy survived, but the doctors said he would need multiple surgeries and might never walk normally again. Mai was never charged—the family's lawyer made it clear the boy had run out without warning—but that did not matter to her.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of the accident came back to her not as a story she could tell but as a series of pictures that appeared without warning: the boy's startled face just before impact, the unnatural angle of his leg, the mother's hands flying up to her mouth. Loud noises of any kind could set it off—a car horn in traffic, a door slamming in the salon—and she would feel her heart race, her palms go slick with sweat, and for a moment she would be right back on that street corner. Sometimes, when the images came, she would feel nothing at all. She would recall the whole scene with a strange, hollow numbness, as if it had happened to someone else, as if she were watching a movie. And then, just as suddenly, the grief would hit her—a raw, wordless sorrow that made her want to curl up on the floor and cry for that boy and his mother and for herself, for the person she used to be before she had done this.

Mai stopped driving completely. She asked her boyfriend to drive her to work, or she took the bus, even if it meant an extra forty minutes each way—but she never felt at ease accepting the rides. Every time her boyfriend said yes, she found herself waiting for the moment he would sigh or cancel or tell her she was being ridiculous. She had come to believe that other people could not really be counted on, not in the long run. Her boyfriend was kind, but she was certain he would eventually grow tired of her needs, just as she was certain that if she ever told her coworkers the full story, they would pull back or judge her silently. Even when her manager offered to adjust her schedule after the panic attack, Mai nodded and said it was fine, privately convinced that the offer would be withdrawn if she actually took it. She had learned, she told herself, that depending on others was a risk she could not afford—the one person she had failed to protect was a child she had never met, and if she could not trust herself, how could she trust anyone else?

At the salon, Mai became excessively compliant. When a client complained about the cut, she apologized and offered a free redo even when the cut was fine. When her coworker asked her to stay late, she said yes even though she was exhausted. She had come to believe that she could not trust herself—if her own body could cause such harm without her intending it, then she had no right to assert herself, to say no. She had failed to protect that boy, so she would try to protect everyone else now by never causing any friction, never being a problem. This fawn response had started to drain her. She would go home and lie on the couch, unable to relax even in her own bedroom, because she was always scanning for threats. In the salon, she had memorized the location of every exit the first day she returned to work. In a restaurant with her boyfriend, she would sit facing the door, her eyes darting to the back hallway every few minutes. He had started to ask why she seemed so on edge, and she did not know how to explain that her body had become a liability, that she no longer trusted herself to be safe around others—and that even as she accepted his rides and his comfort, she was bracing for the moment he would stop giving them.

What finally brought Mai to seek help was a panic attack that hit her in the middle of a haircut. A client had brought her toddler, and the child slipped off the chair and let out a sharp cry. Mai heard it and froze, the sound dissolving into the memory of the boy's wail. She dropped her scissors and had to run to the back room, her hands shaking, her chest tight. The salon manager asked if she was okay, and Mai said yes, but she knew she was not. She made an appointment with a therapist that afternoon, though part of her was already skeptical that talking would help—why would a stranger be any different from everyone else who had told her it was not her fault but could not actually make her believe it? What she was most afraid of, she told herself, was that she would never feel normal again—that she would always be this version of herself, jumpy, compliant, grieving, unable to trust either herself or the people around her. But what she hoped for, in a small and barely acknowledged corner of her mind, was that someone could help her understand why she could not let the accident go, even though everyone else had told her it was not her fault.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Avoid Anniversaries: The vignette does not mention avoiding any dates or anniversaries connected to the traumatic event.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
